### Proposed working group name

Agent Context and Memory Working Group

### One-sentence summary (elevator pitch, ~25 words max)

Define standards and best practices for context management and agent memory that supports agent workshops and harnesses.

### Detailed description of the working group's focus and scope

Develop vendor-neutral standards and practices for how agents acquire, organize, retrieve, retain, and share context and memory across tasks, sessions, and systems. Cover context graphs, knowledge graphs, vector retrieval, structured and unstructured stores, and hybrid approaches, alongside context compression, memory lifecycle management, and evaluation. Recommendations will apply across models, agent harnesses, deployment environments, and industries.

### Problem statement — what challenge or gap does this address?

Agent context and memory implementations use inconsistent terminology, representations, lifecycle rules, and evaluation methods, making them difficult to compare or connect. Existing work on retrieval, knowledge representation, and agent interfaces provides foundations, but shared guidance is needed for combining these capabilities across agent systems. During charter development, we will validate this gap against existing AAIF and external initiatives and narrow the scope wherever responsibilities overlap.

### Why is this relevant to Agentic AI specifically?

Agents must preserve task state, learn from prior interactions, and select relevant information while operating across tools, sessions, and collaborators. Unlike a single model response, a sustained agent workflow requires explicit decisions about what to remember, when to retrieve it, how to update it, and whom to trust. These decisions directly affect task completion, consistency, security, latency, and cost.

### Proposed goals and intended outcomes

- Establish shared terminology and a reference architecture for agent context and memory.
- Define portable representations and lifecycle semantics that support interoperability across agent harnesses and storage technologies.
- Publish practical guidance for selecting, assembling, compressing, and maintaining context.
- Develop evaluation methods for memory quality, task outcomes, security, latency, and cost.
- Validate recommendations through open examples spanning multiple implementations and industry use cases.

### How does this align with the Agentic AI Foundation's mission?

The group will support an open, interoperable agent ecosystem by developing shared foundations for context and memory across projects and vendors. Public specifications, implementation guidance, and evaluations will lower adoption barriers and enable contributors to build compatible systems. Open participation and transparent development will keep the work grounded in broad community needs.

### Key topics or workstreams to be covered

- Memory models and representation: working, episodic, semantic, and procedural memory; context graphs, knowledge graphs, vector indexes, relational stores, documents, and files.
- Context management: retrieval, ranking, assembly, compression, summarization, caching, and token budgeting.
- Memory lifecycle: extraction, consolidation, updates, temporal validity, conflict resolution, retention, and deletion.
- Interoperability and trust: exchange across agent harnesses, shared memory, provenance, access controls, privacy, and defenses against memory poisoning.
- Evaluation and observability: task success, retrieval quality, memory correctness, continuity, latency, and cost.

### Proposed deliverables (e.g., whitepaper, standards, guidelines, tooling)

- Terminology and reference architecture v1 for developers and maintainers, completed through public review with examples covering multiple storage approaches.
- Best-practice guide v1 for application teams, including implementation patterns, tradeoffs, and operational guidance.
- Draft interoperability profile for framework and memory-system maintainers, with schemas and lifecycle semantics demonstrated by at least two independent implementations.
- Evaluation guide and reproducible test scenarios for researchers and practitioners, covering quality, security, latency, and cost.
- Open reference examples for developers, demonstrating representative workflows across multiple harnesses and memory backends.

### First-year delivery timeline

- Months 1–3: Develop the charter for TC approval, map adjacent initiatives, collect use cases, and draft terminology. - Months 4–6: Publish the draft reference architecture and initial best-practice guide for public review. - Months 7–9: Develop the draft interoperability profile, reference integrations, and evaluation scenarios. - Months 10–12: Validate through independent implementations, publish revised deliverables, and propose priorities for annual charter renewal.

### Suggested meeting cadence

Biweekly

### Proposed chair and co-chair

- Chair: Stephen Chin, VP of Developer Relations, Neo4j. AAIF membership tier: Silver
- Co-chair: Tejas Chopra, Headroom. AAIF membership tier: Silver

### Target participants / expertise needed

- Agent framework, harness, and orchestration maintainers.
- Memory, retrieval, knowledge representation, and context engineering researchers.
- Graph, vector, relational, document, and storage infrastructure specialists.
- Security, privacy, governance, and evaluation practitioners.
- Application developers and users across industries, including contributors from non-member organizations.

### Committed participants from at least three organizations

Stephen Chin, Neo4j: Chair the group and contribute expertise in context graphs, knowledge graphs, GraphRAG, and developer adoption.
Tejas Chopra, Headroom: Co-chair the group and contribute to context management, efficiency, and implementation guidance.
Vasilije Markovic, Founder @ Cognee: Expert in memory systems, agentic harnesses, and graph memory retrieval

### Ideal working group size

10-15 members

### Overlap and coordination with AAIF WGs and external bodies

Relevant coordination targets include MCP for context and tool interfaces, A2A for agent collaboration, and W3C knowledge representation and provenance standards. We will ask the AAIF TC to identify adjacent WGs during charter development and establish shared reviews or workstreams where responsibilities overlap. This group will focus on context selection and memory semantics, lifecycle, portability, and evaluation, reusing existing protocols and standards wherever possible.

### Who are the primary beneficiaries of this work?

Agent developers, framework and harness maintainers, memory and data infrastructure providers, researchers, and organizations deploying agents. End users will benefit from more consistent task execution, clearer control over retained information, and better continuity across interactions.

### Anticipated impact (technical / policy / industry / societal)

Technically, the work should improve interoperability, memory quality, and context efficiency while reducing repeated integration work. Across industries, shared evaluation methods and implementation guidance should make architectural choices easier to assess and reduce switching costs. Provenance, access controls, and lifecycle guidance should also strengthen accountability and user control over agent memory.

### Urgency — why now?

Long-running and multi-agent workflows make context and memory architectural concerns rather than simple prompt configuration. Establishing shared foundations while implementations are evolving can reduce fragmentation and make future systems easier to connect. Early collaboration also creates an opportunity to address provenance, deletion, and access control before incompatible practices become entrenched.

### Are there risks or challenges to this working group succeeding?

The main risks are excessive scope, inconsistent terminology, vendor-specific assumptions, and benchmarks that fail to reflect real workloads. We will mitigate these through phased deliverables, a bounded initial interoperability profile, diverse contributors, and validation across independent implementations. Recommendations will distinguish established practices from open research questions.

### Estimated resource needs (budget, tooling, staff support)

Initial needs are contributor time, a public repository, meeting infrastructure, and light AAIF coordination support; no dedicated budget is proposed at launch. Reference implementations and evaluations may require modest compute and hosting, with specific needs scoped before resources are committed.

### Existing work and supporting references (if any)

The group will build on existing research and implementations in retrieval-augmented generation, GraphRAG, agent memory, context compression, and knowledge representation. Starting references include MCP (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/), A2A (https://a2a-protocol.org/), W3C PROV (https://www.w3.org/TR/prov-overview/), and W3C RDF (https://www.w3.org/RDF/). An initial landscape review will identify reusable work and remaining interoperability gaps.

### Supporting documents or attachments

No supporting attachments at this stage. A draft charter, use-case inventory, and landscape review will be developed openly during the Sandbox phase.

### Links to relevant references or resources

- Model Context Protocol: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/
- Agent2Agent Protocol: https://a2a-protocol.org/
- W3C Provenance: https://www.w3.org/TR/prov-overview/
- W3C Resource Description Framework: https://www.w3.org/RDF/
- GraphRAG reference implementation: https://github.com/microsoft/graphrag

### Additional comments

The group will remain vendor-neutral and industry-agnostic, with no required database, model provider, or agent framework. Initial priorities will be refined with participants and the TC during Sandbox charter development, with emphasis on practical deliverables and independently demonstrated interoperability.
